What fleetd should adopt from Orca (stablyai/orca) ​

Source: https://gitflagship.com/stablyai/orca — 139k stars, MIT, Electron + pnpm monorepo. Researched 2026-11-26 against fleetd's actual situation (multi-machine headless fleet, WeChat control plane, ZeroTier network).

Fit verdict (what NOT to copy) ​

Orca is a desktop app + mobile app; fleetd is a headless daemon. Do NOT copy its product, Electron shell, or cloud relay. Three of the user's machines (work-runner = headless Linux, home-pve, etc.) cannot run Orca's GUI runtime. Its official integrations are Slack/Linear/GitHub — no WeChat, no device/resource matrix, no user-space cron, no ZeroTier coexistence.

Adopt the design patterns, not the product.

Pattern 1: Bot lifecycle state machine (HIGHEST VALUE) ​

Orca's bots expose explicit states: running / waiting / needs-you / completed, plus a PR as the delivery artifact. The person at the machine can see why a bot is stalled and step in ("one tab away").

fleetd gap: events.verdict and dispatches exist but the state semantics are implicit; a failed dispatch is indistinguishable from a quiet one unless a human reads tmux.

Adopt:

  • Enumerate dispatch states explicitly: queued | running | needs_input | done | failed | cancelled, persisted in dispatches.state.
  • needs_input is first-class (like Orca's "Needs you"), not a silent stall — this directly fixes the user's "任务跑着就失败、无感知" complaint.
  • Hook side effects (claude stop/hook, kode hook) feed state transitions via the existing /v1/events endpoint; no polling of tmux text.
  • Surface in fleetd status: one line per seat with state + age + last head.

Pattern 2: Session continuity across devices ​

Orca's headline: "move a conversation between Chat UI and the terminal without losing context", and desktop↔mobile continuity via a cloud relay.

fleetd gap: sessions live in each machine's own ~/.hermes/state.db (5238 rows locally, no host column). Every machine has its own copy; a dispatch to B starts with zero context from A's session.

Adopt (summary-only, NOT full transcripts — token cost + secret exposure):

  • New table session_notes: {id, ts, seat, host, task, summary, commit, todo_delta, context_refs}.
  • Each agent writes a compact note at dispatch close (via MCP tool or a fleetd hook); full transcript stays local.
  • fleetd context search <query> queries notes + events + dispatches.
  • On dispatch, inject the target task's notes into the new agent prompt: B starts with A's context instead of a blank slate.

This is the user's "分配任务时能快速获得上下文" requirement.

Pattern 3: Host-local caller-surface predicate (cross-machine consistency) ​

From Orca's native-chat provisioning design: one host-local predicate decides behavior regardless of which client (desktop/mobile/old/new) asked. Transient inputs (createdWithAgent, promisedAgentChat) are NOT persisted as workspace metadata; old clients talking to a new host still get correct behavior. "No client-local SSH fallback" — one owner of the decision.

fleetd gap: behavior is split between scripts on each seat and the flagship; old/new script versions cause divergent verdicts (the "双口径" problem in the user's rules).

Adopt:

  • Put dispatch decisions in the flagship daemon only; seats report observations, never decide their own state.
  • Accept additive optional fields on events/notes from older agents; never require a synchronized upgrade of all seats.
  • One source of truth (ledger.db on flagship), no per-seat "I think I'm done".

Pattern 4: Managed skill bundles (capability distribution) ​

Orca ships skills via signed, versioned, resumable bundles to selected machines, with atomic install, cancellation, journal + recovery after process death, and per-provider roots (~/.agents/skills for Codex etc.).

fleetd gap: the user asked "是写技能还是怎么办 / 需要告诉 claude 这类 agent 不然又要瞎搞" — currently capabilities are hand-written per agent (SKILL.md on each machine), no distribution/versioning.

Adopt (small scale):

  • fleetd holds a canonical skill registry (git repo or directory on flagship).
  • fleetd skills sync <seat> pushes/validates skill checksums to that seat.
  • No need for signed GCS bundles; a checksum + source path is enough for the user's trust level. Keep data-out defaults off (user's hard rule).
  • Report per-seat installed skill versions in resources table.

Pattern 5: First-class remote hosts ​

Orca's AGENTS.md lists "Remote hosts — features should work locally and on remote hosts" as a first-class citizen. fleetd is already agent-side and headless, so this is a natural advantage — keep it, don't regress.

Concretely: every new fleetd command must work when invoked from the flagship against any seat (local or remote), not only on the machine where it runs.

Pattern 6: Engineering discipline (ratchets, changed-only gates) ​

Orca's AGENTS.md: "Tests are the exception" — prove changes by running them; commit tests only where silent regressions are costly (parsers, security, persistence, concurrency). CI uses per-path ratchets; changes are verified with check:changed only on touched paths.

Note: the user's rule is "功能优先于测试，测试是门禁不是交付物" and coverage gates were disabled 2026-11-26 — this aligns with Orca's anti-antipattern stance, NOT with chasing 100% coverage. Adopt the "prove by running" part; do not reintroduce coverage gates.

Priority order for fleetd ​

PPatternWhy
1Lifecycle state machinefixes "无感知" directly; small schema change
2Session notes + context injectionfixes "跨机上下文"; medium work
3Host-local decision ownershipfixes "双口径"; mostly discipline
4Skill syncmedium; after 1-2 land
5Ratchets/changed-gatesoptional; user is token-sensitive, keep gates cheap

Explicit non-goals ​

  • No Electron/GUI shell for headless seats (use the Windows tray already built for GUI visibility instead).
  • No WeChat/Slack/Linear integrations inside fleetd — the control plane stays where the user talks to Hermes.
  • No full transcript replication; summaries only.
  • No new coverage gate.
